timed_text.text: Day 21. When you face a challenge, your brain does something automatic.
It imagines the worst case — failure, loss, the fear scenario.
That's not weakness.
That's your nervous system doing exactly what it was designed to do.
That threat response is ancient.
It was built to keep you alive.
It fires the same way — facing a predator or stepping to the starting line.
There are two types of athletes in those moments.
The victim and the fighter.
The victim acknowledges the fear and becomes it.
They make excuses.
They shrink.
They find reasons why the situation is unfair or why they're not ready.
And they stay on the safe side of the line.
The fighter acknowledges the same fear and steps over the line anyway.
They've decided the fear doesn't get to make the call.
The difference isn't talent.
It isn't physical preparation.
A decision made in seconds: who's in charge — you or the fear?
You or the fear?
You've been building the tools to make that decision automatically.
Today we name it explicitly.
On screen — identify your line and declare which side you choose.

cards.prompt: Describe the fear you feel before your most challenging competitive moments. Be specific — what does it say? What worst-case scenario does your brain go to?
Now name it for what it is — your brain trying to protect you. It's not the truth. It's a signal.
The fighter steps over the line anyway. What does stepping over the line look like for you — specifically, in the moment that fear arrives?
